"Mince" has three distinct meanings, and here's something beautiful: they all quietly share one core idea — reducing something to something smaller or less forceful than it naturally is. Once you see that thread, all three meanings lock into place permanently.
Meaning 1: To cut food into extremely tiny pieces

This is the most common, everyday meaning. When you mince something, you cut it so finely that it's reduced to near-microscopic crumbles — far beyond ordinary chopping.

To put it in perspective: slicing makes large flat pieces, chopping makes rough irregular pieces, dicing makes neat small cubes — but mincing goes all the way down to the smallest possible fragments, almost paste-like.

Garlic is probably the most commonly minced food in the world. When a recipe says "mince three cloves of garlic," it means you should chop them so fine that they practically melt and disappear into whatever you're cooking. Fresh herbs like parsley, ginger, chillies, and meat (particularly in dishes like shepherd's pie or Bolognese sauce) are also frequently minced.

"Minced" can function as an adjective too, describing the result: minced garlic, minced beef, minced herbs.
Meaning 2: To walk with unnaturally tiny, dainty, overly careful steps

When someone minces while walking, they take small, delicate, affected steps — as if performing elegance rather than simply being elegant. This word carries a mildly mocking or critical tone when used this way. It suggests the walk looks theatrical or excessive, not natural.

"She minced across the polished floor in her tight skirt and heels."

This doesn't compliment her walk. It says her walk looked artificial — overly careful, precious, even slightly ridiculous. The key feeling is pretension: someone trying too hard to appear refined.
Meaning 3: To soften or water down your words (almost always used in the negative)

This is arguably the most important meaning for everyday English communication, and you will encounter it almost exclusively in the negative form.

When you "mince words," you choose your language carefully to avoid stating something directly — you dance around the truth, soften an uncomfortable message, or speak vaguely to avoid upsetting someone.

The phrase you'll see constantly is "not mince words" or "didn't mince words," meaning the exact opposite: speaking with full directness and bluntness, without softening anything.

"She didn't mince words — she told him exactly why the project had failed."
This means she was completely honest, with no sugarcoating.

Saying someone did mince their words, on the other hand, implies evasiveness or excessive diplomacy:

"He minced his words, not wanting to hurt her feelings, but she understood what he really meant."

A slightly more formal variant — "not to mince matters" — carries the same meaning.

All three meanings reduce something:

  • Mince food → reduce it to the tiniest possible pieces
  • Mince while walking → reduce your steps to tiny, cautious movements
  • Mince your words → reduce the force and directness of what you say

The word "mince" always implies a kind of shrinking — a making-small. Whether it's garlic under a knife, feet on a floor, or hard truths in a conversation, something full-sized is being cut down into something smaller and more delicate. That's the soul of the word.
